title: Best content optimization tools for ROI-focused teams
content:
Organic search still delivers some of the strongest returns in marketing, and the right content optimization tools make it easier to capture.
But in 2026, the stakes are higher than they used to be. AI search engines like Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and ChatGPT are now a standard part of the buyer research process, and they don’t select sources the same way traditional search does. Marketing teams that optimize only for Google rankings often find themselves invisible in AI-generated answers — and being invisible in AI answers means invisible to buyers.
This guide covers the best content optimization tools available in 2026, organized by use case. Whether the goal is to build a content stack from scratch or to fill gaps in an existing content optimization workflow , this guide breaks down what each tool does and who it’s best for.
Content optimization tools improve content quality, search visibility, and conversion performance. Plenty of content and SEO analysis tools are on the market, and many of them cover a wide range of functions.
Before we get into specific recommendations for AI content optimization tools, here’s a breakdown of the major categories:
HubSpot pro tip: As AI visibility becomes a standard reporting requirement, tools that track it become more important. HubSpot AEO shows where a brand appears in AI-generated answers across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini — and connects that data to the same CRM where the team is already tracking leads and pipeline.
The most effective content stacks combine SEO optimization software with specialized tools for research, AI visibility, and reporting. The breakdowns below are organized by category, covering what each tool does, who it’s best for, and how it fits into a content stack.
These tools analyze and score content against top-ranking competitors, surfacing specific recommendations to close gaps. Most use NLP and semantic analysis rather than simple keyword density.
HubSpot’s SEO Marketing Software is built into Marketing Hub and provides teams with a centralized view of SEO performance, on-page recommendations, and topic cluster structure. It’s all connected to the same CRM data that powers the rest of HubSpot’s platform.
Unlike standalone SEO tools, HubSpot’s SEO recommendations are tied directly to a brand’s actual content and pages. Teams can see which pages need optimization, act on those recommendations within the same platform, and track the downstream impact on traffic and leads without switching between tools or manually stitching together data.
What I like: The biggest advantage isn’t the recommendations themselves (which are solid) — it’s that they’re connected to real pipeline data. When a content team can show that improving a cluster of pages drove a measurable increase in marketing-qualified lead (MQL) volume, securing executive buy-in for SEO investment becomes much easier.
Best for: Marketing teams already on HubSpot who want integrated SEO visibility without managing a separate tool. Ideal for mid-market and enterprise teams that need to report on content ROI across the full funnel.
Pro tip: Teams on Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise can add AEO through the HubSpot for Marketers bundle, keeping SEO and AI search visibility in one platform.
What the experts say : Rob Freedman , VP of Marketing at SureCam, said, “I use HubSpot’s content editor, SEO recommendations, and content calendar to plan, publish, and optimize website and blog content, then tie each asset directly to campaigns so I can report on pipeline and revenue impact in our CRM.”
Clearscope is a content discoverability platform covering the full content workflow: topic research, AI-assisted drafting, on-page optimization, content monitoring, internal linking, and AI search visibility tracking across ChatGPT and Gemini.
What I like: Clearscope’s interface is clean and fast, which makes it one of the easier tools to standardize across a writing team. The query fan-out feature is useful for an AI search strategy, helping teams understand the downstream searches that AI platforms trigger to build their answers. It also gives content teams a concrete signal for where to invest.
Best for: Enterprise content teams and agency partners who want a unified platform for on-page optimization and AI search visibility, with unlimited user seats and no per-seat pricing.
What the experts say: Cassy Aite , co-founder of Postbeam.ai and Hoppier.com, said, “Clearscope has been a huge part of how I scale content with new writers. It helps both me and the writer reduce the amount of on page seo research for content, which cuts down the editing process and gives me more confidence that the content is actually optimized before it goes live.”
Surfer is an AI visibility platform that combines on-page content optimization with AI search tracking, topical authority planning, and competitive intelligence across Google and major AI engines, including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews.
Pricing: Starts at $119/month billed monthly, or $99/month billed annually.
What I like: The Mention Gap feature is a useful addition for teams building an AI search strategy. Knowing specifically which AI engines are citing competitors for a given topic gives teams a concrete starting point for closing visibility gaps rather than optimizing unquestioningly.
Best for: Content teams and SEO specialists who want a unified platform for on-page optimization and AI visibility tracking, with strong support for high-volume publishing and multi-brand management.
What the experts say: Chris Coussons , founder at Visionary Marketing, tests tools out before fully committing to adding them to the martech stack. This is what he said about Surfer SEO:
“We did a test of Surfer SEO at the end of last year, and optimised 50% of a client’s aged blogs with their content optimization, and left the other 50% as they were, and measured the impact. The uplift on the optimized blogs was higher than I think everyone expected, with an average increase of 4 places (zero for the control) and 43% clicks in the 3 months that followed. We’ve used it ever since on all of our clients’ blogs.”
Optimization starts before writing begins. This category covers tools that help teams plan more strategically, produce better briefs, and accelerate first-draft creation, while keeping content grounded in real keyword and intent data.
HubSpot’s CMS platform with built-in AI content creation, drag-and-drop editing, and content optimization features designed for teams that want to build, publish, and optimize content in a single environment.
Content Hub helps content teams publish faster, but its bigger advantage is structural: the AI content writer produces clear, extractable content that both human readers and AI search engines can parse and cite. That structure aligns with how generative engines evaluate and pull from sources.
For teams trying to optimize for Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), this integration between the CMS and the AI writing layer is a meaningful structural advantage. Teams aren’t retrofitting AI optimization onto a legacy CMS; the capability is already built into the content creation workflow.
Best for: Teams that want a unified platform for building, publishing, optimizing, and measuring content without stitching together separate CMS, SEO, and AI tools.
HubSpot pro tip: Content Hub and Marketing Hub are separate products, but they’re designed to work together. Teams that want both traditional SEO and AEO in one platform can access them through the HubSpot for Marketers bundle, which combines both hubs and includes AEO — all connected to the same CRM data.
What the experts say: Kshitij Chaudhary , founder of Dintellects, relies heavily on HubSpot’s content tools. He said, “I love using the HubSpot Content Tools. It helps me to organize how I work with content and see how my blog posts are doing. I can see how they are helping me generate leads and improve my search rankings. The tool is extremely helpful because it keeps all my content and marketing work in one place.”
Frase is an agentic SEO and GEO platform that consolidates research, writing, optimization, AI-driven visibility tracking, and content maintenance into a single platform. Frase covers the full content strategy, from SERP research and brief creation through AI-powered drafting, combined SEO + GEO scoring, and automated content decay detection.
Pricing: Starts at $49/month billed monthly, or $39/month billed annually.
What I like: Instead of optimizing for Google in one tool and then checking AI visibility separately, Frase gives marketers a single score that accounts for both. This is helpful for teams that have been asking, “Are we optimizing for the right things now that AI search matters?”
Best for: Content teams that want to consolidate a fragmented tool stack into one platform covering research, writing, SEO, GEO, and AI visibility tracking.
What the experts say: Chaudhary is also a Frase user. He said, “I use this tool for quick content research. It helps me to create outlines for my articles and to discover what people are looking for online. I can see what questions people have and what they want to know about something. It helps me write my articles.”
MarketMuse is a content intelligence platform that uses AI to identify content gaps, prioritize topics, and score content quality across an entire website.
Pricing: Free plan available; paid plans are quote-based.
What I like: MarketMuse helps marketers quickly create an entire content library covering target topics and highest-priority gaps. For content teams, this tool can help prevent duplication and focus effort where it will have the most strategic impact.
Best for: Enterprise and mid-market teams managing content libraries of 100+ pages who need a strategic, site-wide view of their content gaps.
Strong internal linking helps search engines understand topical authority, improves crawlability, and passes equity between related pages, all of which compound over time. Here are some tools that can help marketers optimize site structure.
HubSpot’s topic cluster tool visualizes how pillar pages and cluster content connect across a site. It flags missing links, identifies orphaned content, and makes it straightforward to build the kind of semantic architecture that search engines — and AI engines — reward.
Unlike standalone site auditing tools, the topic cluster map is built directly into Marketing Hub, so the recommendations connect to the same pages, contacts, and pipeline data that the rest of the team is already working from. When a cluster improves, the impact shows up in the same dashboard where leads and revenue are tracked. Topic clusters are available across Marketing Hub Starter, Pro, and Enterprise.
What I like: The visual map makes it easy to present site structure to stakeholders who aren’t deep in SEO. Being able to show the connection between strategic topics and actual content in a single view tends to accelerate alignment on content priorities — and makes it much easier to argue for investing in gap content.
Best for: Marketing teams already on HubSpot who want a strategic view of their content architecture without managing a separate site auditing tool. Particularly useful for teams building or expanding topic clusters as part of an AI search visibility strategy.
Link Whisper is a WordPress plugin that uses AI to suggest and insert internal links as content is written, with site-level reporting for orphaned pages, broken links, and link structure.
What I like: Link Whisper removes the manual work of internal linking without requiring a strategic overhaul. The GSC integration is a useful addition, too, since it surfaces the terms Google already associates with a brand’s pages as linking targets.
Best for: WordPress-based content teams with large archives who want to improve internal linking without a manual audit process. Not suited for non-WordPress sites.
What the experts say: Keran Smith , Co-Founder and Chief Marketing Officer at LYFE Marketing, said, “Link Whisper saves me hours by letting me implement anchor text across multiple keywords with a single click. We have thousands of pages on our site, so it helps us improve our anchor text efforts at scale.”
Screaming Frog is a technical SEO crawler for Windows, macOS, and Linux that audits site structure, identifies over 300 SEO issues, and surfaces internal linking gaps.
What I like: No other tool gives the same depth of crawl data at this price point. Screaming Frog’s AI integration allows SEO teams to run content quality checks or custom extraction prompts at scale during a crawl, without building a separate workflow.
Best for: SEO specialists and technical teams who need a deep site crawl before or after a major content push, site migration, or CMS change.
What the experts say: For Robertas Voroneckis , Head of SEO and Growth at Demo Agency, Screaming Frog is a non-negotiable. “Screaming Frog is my go-to for technical SEO audits because it gives a very detailed view of crawl issues, metadata, internal linking, indexation signals, and site structure,” he said.
Publishing is just the beginning of content optimization. This category covers tools that help teams test what’s working and audit existing content before republishing.
Hotjar, now part of Contentsquare, is a behavior analytics platform that shows how real users interact with content pages through heatmaps, session recordings, funnels, and on-page surveys.
Pricing: Free plan available. Paid plans start at $49/month billed monthly, or $39/month billed annually.
What I like: Hotjar answers a question most content optimization tools can’t: do the people who land on a page actually read it, engage with it, and understand it? For content teams running optimization sprints, combining heatmap data with post-publish performance metrics closes the loop between content quality and user behavior in a way that pure SEO scoring can’t.
Best for: Content and demand gen teams who want behavioral data to inform content QA and page-level optimization decisions. Particularly useful for high-traffic landing pages, pillar content, and any page being tested for conversion improvements.
What the experts say: Smith also uses Hotjar in his content optimization toolbox. He said, “Hotjar plays an important role in helping us understand and improve our website UI and UX. The ability to view actual recordings of how our website visitors navigate the site is extremely insightful.”
Google Search Console is Google’s free tool for monitoring search performance, including clicks, impressions, CTR, and average position by query and page.
What I like: Search Console is the baseline. The query data is particularly useful for identifying content that’s close to ranking but underperforming.
What the experts say: Voroneckis said, “Google Search Console is usually my starting point because it shows how a business is already being found, which pages have traction, and where the easiest optimization opportunities are.”
Proving that content drives pipeline is one of the hardest problems in marketing. Here are some content optimization tools that can help close the gap between publishing and performance reporting.
HubSpot’s AEO tool helps marketing teams understand where and how their brand appears in AI-generated answers across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini — and what’s driving or limiting that visibility.
In 2026, ranking in traditional search and being cited in AI answers are two different outcomes that require different signals. A page can rank on page one and still be absent from ChatGPT responses, Perplexity answers, or Gemini results for the same query. HubSpot AEO surfaces where a brand appears in AI answers, identifies the content and entity signals influencing visibility, and provides teams with a structured way to track progress over time.
Demand generation leaders increasingly need to connect content investment to pipeline, and AEO visibility metrics — citations, share of AI answers, coverage by topic — are now a required reporting layer alongside traditional SEO metrics.
Pricing: HubSpot AEO starts at $50/month (or $45/month billed annually) and includes a free 28-day trial, no credit card required. Teams on Marketing Hub Professional or Enterprise get deeper CRM integration and built-in content tools alongside AEO.
What I like: HubSpot AEO connects AI visibility data to the same platform where marketing teams track SEO, content, CRM, and pipeline. That integration is what makes the data useful rather than just interesting — it becomes possible to see not just where the brand appears in AI answers, but what content and entity-building activities are driving that visibility.
HubSpot pro tip: HubSpot AEO is available with HubSpot Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise. Marketing teams that combine HubSpot SEO tools with AEO get a unified view of traditional and AI search performance — which is the only way to accurately measure the full impact of a content investment in 2026.
Semrush is an all-in-one digital marketing platform that covers SEO, AI-driven visibility tracking, competitive intelligence, content optimization, advertising, and PR.
Pricing: Starts at $139.95/month billed monthly, or $117.33/month billed annually.
What I like: The addition of the AI Visibility Toolkit and Semrush One bundle means teams don’t have to manage separate tools to track both traditional search rankings and AI citation visibility.
Best for: Mid-market and enterprise SEO and content teams who need a full-suite platform for organic strategy, competitive intelligence, and AI visibility tracking in one place.
What the experts say: Chaudhary is a fan of Semrush. He said, “I use this tool for finding keywords and seeing what my competitors are doing. I use Semrush to plan what I will write about and to see how my website is doing over time. Semrush helps me make a plan for my website.”
Ahrefs is an AI marketing platform that combines SEO intelligence, backlink analysis, content research, and AI-driven search visibility tracking.
Pricing: Starts at $129/month billed monthly, or $108/month billed annually.
What I like: Ahrefs’ Content Explorer is useful for content strategy work. Marketers can use it to search for the highest-traffic content on any topic, filtered by date, domain rating, and linking domains, and it surfaces competitive gaps that keyword research alone misses.
Best for: SEO strategists and content teams who need deep competitive intelligence alongside keyword and backlink data, and who want AI visibility tracking built into the same platform rather than managed separately.
[ Looking for more tools? Check out this list of 53 free content writing tools to level up your workflow.]
Content optimization tools support research, brief creation, on-page optimization, testing, and reporting. SEO optimization tools cover a broader range of search tasks, such as keyword research, audits, tracking, and technical analysis.
Most high-performing content teams use both SEO tools to set strategic direction and identify opportunities, and content optimization tools to ensure that what gets published is competitive enough to perform.
Google Search Console is free and provides the baseline performance data behind any content optimization effort. For content teams with real optimization needs, a paid tool is typically necessary to get the depth of competitive analysis and keyword coverage required.
HubSpot’s SEO tools, Content Hub, and AEO platform integrate natively, so no data sync is required, and performance metrics connect directly to contacts, pipeline, and revenue. Among third-party tools, Semrush and Ahrefs both offer HubSpot integrations that surface keyword and performance data within the CRM.
The most reliable approach is to establish a performance baseline before using a tool, then measure changes in organic sessions, keyword rankings, leads generated, and pipeline influenced over a 90-day minimum period. For AI search specifically, content teams should track changes in brand citation frequency across major AI platforms alongside traditional search metrics. Tools like HubSpot that connect content performance to CRM data make this attribution significantly more straightforward.
AI content optimization tools speed up drafting, surface recommendations, and automate workflows. For teams already using HubSpot, Content Hub’s AI content writer handles brief creation, drafting, and on-page optimization in a single environment, reducing the number of tools a small team needs to manage.
Content optimization is a system that spans strategy, creation, structure, and measurement, not a single step in the publishing process.
I’ve worked with content teams at various stages of maturity, and the ones that get the best results treat content optimization as a discipline. And it starts with better tools and a clear system for using them.
For most content teams, that means full-stack content optimization runs through HubSpot because it connects the pieces that typically get siloed: SEO recommendations, AI writing, AEO visibility, and CRM-attributed performance reporting.
For content teams unsure where to start, the Content Marketing Planning Templates are a great first step toward building a structured, measurable content program that makes optimization work.

title: 6 best CRMs for wholesalers in 2026
content:
Wholesale businesses require more than a generic customer relationship management (CRM) system. A CRM for wholesalers must support account-specific pricing, large product catalogs, repeat orders, and sales workflows that integrate with inventory and fulfillment systems. When these processes are disconnected, quoting slows, errors increase, and revenue opportunities are harder to capture.
The best CRM for wholesale distributors connects customer data with pricing logic, order workflows, and inventory visibility. This setup allows sales teams to move from quote to order without switching systems, while giving operations leaders accurate pipeline insight and enabling field reps to work effectively from mobile devices.
This guide compares the best CRM software for wholesalers in 2026. The guide evaluates each platform based on wholesale-specific requirements like enterprise resource planning (ERP) and inventory integration, mobile field sales capabilities, pricing flexibility, and total cost of ownership.
A CRM for wholesalers is a customer relationship management system designed to support B2B distribution workflows, including account-specific pricing, bulk ordering, and sales processes integrated with inventory and fulfillment systems. It helps wholesale teams manage accounts, generate accurate quotes, and move orders forward without relying on disconnected tools.
Wholesale CRM software supports customer-specific pricing and tiered price lists, allowing distributors to apply contract pricing, volume discounts, and negotiated terms at the account level. It also connects sales workflows to inventory and order status data, typically through integrations with ERP systems.
In practice, the CRM system manages accounts, contacts, deals, and sales activity, while the ERP system manages inventory, purchasing, and fulfillment. This separation allows wholesale teams to maintain accurate operational data while giving sales teams the context they need to quote and sell efficiently. Many of these requirements overlap with those in manufacturing environments , where CRM systems also connect sales activity to production and fulfillment processes.
Wholesale distribution introduces requirements that standard CRMs do not fully support without additional configuration or integrations. These differences affect how teams price, sell, and fulfill orders.
Wholesale CRM requirements often overlap with adjacent industries like retail, but differ in pricing models, order volume, and account structure. See this guide to the best CRMs for retail for a comparison of customer-focused sales environments.
The right CRM helps wholesale teams reduce quoting delays, connect sales activity with inventory data, and give reps clearer account visibility. The six CRM platforms below address different wholesale needs, from field sales and stock-aware quoting to enterprise forecasting and ERP connectivity.
HubSpot Smart CRM is HubSpot’s AI-powered system of record for account, contact, deal, and activity data. For wholesale distributors, it can support quote-to-order workflows through product libraries, quotes, workflows, reporting, and integrations with ERP, inventory, and order management systems.
HubSpot also connects Smart CRM with Commerce Hub and Breeze, HubSpot’s collection of AI tools, so wholesale teams can manage customer data, quoting, billing, payments, automation, and reporting from a shared customer record.
Best for: Wholesalers who want a single platform to manage sales, service, and marketing while connecting to ERP and inventory systems
What we like: Combines a unified customer database with automation, AI, and flexible integrations, making it easier to manage complex B2B relationships without adding operational overhead.
Pepperi combines CRM, B2B commerce, mobile order taking, and field sales tools for wholesale distributors and brands. Sales reps and buyers can use Pepperi to access customer-specific catalogs, price lists, promotions, and order workflows from web and mobile experiences.
Pepperi fits distributors that need stronger field sales execution, offline mobile access, route-based selling, and customer-specific buying experiences.
Best for: Wholesale distributors that need a combined CRM, B2B commerce platform, and field sales solution
What we like: Built specifically for wholesale operations, with comprehensive support for mobile sales reps, order taking, and customer-specific catalogs
Prospect CRM is a stock-aware CRM built for product-selling B2B businesses. It connects customer, product, sales, and inventory data, enabling wholesale teams to quote, manage accounts, and prioritize sales activity with better visibility into stock and buying patterns.
The platform works especially well for distributors that need CRM records to reflect real product movement, repeat orders, backorders, and cross-sell opportunities.
Best for: Wholesalers who need real-time inventory visibility embedded directly in the CRM
What we like: Purpose-built “stock-aware CRM” that connects sales activity with inventory data, helping reps sell based on what is actually available
Zoho CRM is a customizable CRM for small- and mid-sized wholesale teams that need sales automation, pipeline management, territory management, and integrations without enterprise-level pricing. Wholesale teams can connect Zoho CRM with Zoho Inventory and other Zoho apps to manage sales activity alongside inventory and order workflows.
Zoho CRM works best for cost-conscious teams that can configure their own workflows and integrations, or that already use other Zoho products.
Best for: Small to mid-sized wholesalers looking for an affordable CRM with flexible customization and integrations
What we like: Strong balance of price and functionality, with process automation and optional inventory integration through the Zoho ecosystem
Salesforce Sales Cloud, presented by Salesforce as part of Agentforce Sales, serves sales teams that need deep customization, AI, forecasting, territory management, products, price books, and app integrations. Wholesale distributors can configure Salesforce for complex account structures, pricing models, approval workflows, and multi-team coverage.
Salesforce usually fits larger distributors with the budget and internal resources to support implementation, administration, and ongoing customization.
Best for: Enterprise wholesalers with complex territory structures, pricing models, and customization needs
What we like: Highly configurable platform with powerful tools for territory forecasting, product pricing structures, and ecosystem integrations
Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales is Microsoft’s CRM for sales teams that already work in the Microsoft ecosystem. Wholesale distributors can pair Dynamics 365 Sales with Microsoft 365, Power BI, Teams, and Dynamics ERP tools to connect sales activity with product, pricing, quote, order, and fulfillment context.
The platform works best for wholesalers that already use Microsoft tools or want CRM and ERP workflows to sit closer together.
Best for: Wholesalers already using Microsoft tools or requiring tight integration between CRM and ERP systems
What we like: Strong alignment between CRM, ERP, and productivity tools, with built-in support for pricing models and sales territories
Wholesale CRM software improves how teams quote, sell, and manage accounts by connecting customer data with pricing, inventory, and order workflows. For distributors managing high order volume, repeat purchases, and complex pricing structures, a CRM helps reduce manual work while improving visibility across the sales cycle.
Wholesale teams often rely on multiple systems to build quotes, check pricing, confirm inventory, and process orders. These scattered systems create delays, duplicate work, and inaccurate customer information.
CRM software streamlines this process in several ways:
Where HubSpot fits: HubSpot supports creating quotes directly from deals and automates follow-ups and approvals through workflows. With Commerce Hub, teams can manage quoting, billing, and payments in one system, reducing friction between sales and finance.
Wholesale growth depends heavily on repeat orders and long-term account relationships. Without a CRM, account history, communication, and purchasing patterns are often scattered across systems or tied to individual reps. This makes it difficult to maintain continuity when ownership changes or to identify growth opportunities.
A CRM provides a centralized record of every account, including order history, interactions, and engagement across channels. This gives wholesale distribution teams:
Where HubSpot fits: HubSpot’s Smart CRM unifies customer data across teams, making it easier to track account activity and maintain continuity. Workflow automation can trigger reorder reminders or follow-ups based on customer behavior.
For teams handling high volumes of customer communication, CRM functionality often overlaps with call center operations. Explore this guide to the best CRM for call centers for more on managing inbound and outbound interactions.
CRM adoption directly affects revenue by improving sales cycle speed, increasing rep productivity, and providing better visibility into pipeline and account performance. For wholesalers, the largest gains typically come from reducing manual work, capturing more repeat orders, and identifying upsell and cross-sell opportunities.
A CRM also improves forecast accuracy by keeping pipeline data up to date and linking sales activity to revenue outcomes. This allows leadership teams to make more informed decisions about inventory, staffing, and growth planning.
To estimate a CRM system’s ROI impact, wholesale teams often look at:
Even minor improvements across these areas can compound into meaningful revenue gains.
Where HubSpot fits: HubSpot combines pipeline tracking, reporting, and automation into a single platform, helping teams maintain cleaner data and improve forecasting accuracy. AI tools like Breeze assist with prioritization and task execution, reducing the time spent on manual work.
Wholesale CRM software must support complex pricing, high-volume ordering, and sales processes connected to inventory and fulfillment systems. The features below reflect the capabilities most distributors need to manage accounts efficiently and scale operations.
Wholesale CRM software supports account-specific pricing, including contract pricing, volume discounts, and negotiated terms. This ensures quotes reflect agreed pricing without manual adjustments.
HubSpot supports product libraries and quote creation directly from deals, with tiered pricing capabilities available through Commerce Hub.
Wholesale CRM software connects sales workflows to inventory and order data so reps can quote based on available stock and track fulfillment status without switching systems.
HubSpot integrates with inventory and ERP tools through HubSpot Marketplace, enabling shared visibility across systems.
For organizations managing more complex delivery, warehousing, or supply chain workflows, CRM requirements often extend into logistics coordination. See this guide to the best CRMs for logistics businesses for additional options.
HubSpot product libraries help sales teams organize products and add the right items to quotes without having to rebuild catalog information from scratch.
Wholesale teams manage large product catalogs with multiple SKUs, variations, and pricing structures. A CRM should support organizing and accessing this data during sales workflows.
Wholesale operations depend on repeat purchases. CRM software should help teams track buying patterns and trigger follow-ups based on reorder timing. This helps prevent missed reorder opportunities and improves account retention.
HubSpot workflows can automate follow-ups and reminders based on customer behavior or deal activity.
Wholesale sales teams are often structured by region, account coverage, or product line. CRM software should support clear ownership and territory-based reporting.
HubSpot helps teams assign and track account ownership with company records, properties, lists, and reporting views that reflect territory or coverage models.
Field sales reps need access to CRM data while visiting customers, placing orders, or managing accounts on the go.
HubSpot’s mobile app allows reps to manage deals, tasks, and contacts from anywhere.
Wholesale CRM software should connect sales activity to revenue outcomes, helping teams track performance and forecast demand.
HubSpot provides customizable dashboards and reporting tools to track pipeline and sales performance.
Automation reduces manual work and ensures consistency across sales and operational processes. This workflow improvement is especially important for wholesalers managing high order volumes and multi-step approval processes.
HubSpot’s workflow automation enables teams to automate repetitive tasks and streamline handoffs between sales and operations.
Document existing workflows and identify areas where a CRM could improve efficiency. Consider order processing, customer communication, and reporting needs.
List all systems that need to connect with your CRM. Check each platform’s integration options and consider middleware solutions if needed.
Consider subscription fees, implementation costs, training, and ongoing support when evaluating CRM options.
Include representatives from sales, customer service, and operations in the decision-making to ensure the CRM meets all departmental needs.
Use free trials to test CRMs with actual business scenarios. If a free trial isn’t available, book a demo with a sales rep. Create sample quotes, manage test orders, and evaluate ease of use.
Pick a CRM that can grow with your business. HubSpot’s scalable platform allows businesses to start with free tools and add features as they grow.
The best CRM for wholesalers depends on business size, sales complexity, and the degree to which it needs to integrate with inventory, pricing, and order systems.
HubSpot is a strong option for teams that want a unified platform for sales, service, and marketing, with automation, AI tools, and integrations that connect CRM data with ERP and inventory systems. This makes it well-suited for wholesalers looking to streamline quote-to-order workflows and improve visibility across the customer lifecycle.
Wholesale CRM software should support pricing complexity, inventory-connected sales workflows, and repeat ordering. Key features include customer-specific pricing and quoting, ERP and inventory integration, product catalog management, and automated reorder workflows.
Additional capabilities such as territory management, mobile access for field sales teams, revenue-linked reporting, and workflow automation help wholesalers scale operations and maintain accurate pipeline visibility.
Platforms like HubSpot support these features through product libraries, automation, and integrations with inventory and ERP systems.
Yes, HubSpot is suitable for wholesale businesses, particularly those looking to centralize sales, service, and marketing on one platform.
HubSpot supports wholesale workflows through customizable properties, automation, and integrations with ERP and inventory systems. Features like product libraries, quote creation, and Commerce Hub help teams manage pricing and move deals from quote to payment more efficiently. Breeze, HubSpot’s collection of AI tools, also helps teams automate tasks, prioritize opportunities, and maintain cleaner pipeline data, which is critical for managing high-volume, repeat-order sales environments.
CRM costs vary widely depending on features, number of users, and the level of customization required.
For example, Pepperi starts at $500/month for its Pro plan, while Prospect CRM begins at approximately $243 for four users. Zoho CRM offers more affordable per-user pricing starting at $20/user/month, making it a common choice for smaller teams. Enterprise platforms like Salesforce and Microsoft Dynamics 365 typically start at higher per-user price points.
HubSpot offers free tools with CRM functionality , including contact management, deals, and reporting. HubSpot’s Product & Services Catalog lists Smart CRM Starter at $20/month/seat, Smart CRM Professional at $50/month/seat, and Smart CRM Enterprise at $75/month/seat; the current public Smart CRM pricing page also shows annual promotional pricing for Professional at $45/month/seat.
HubSpot stands out as a flexible CRM solution for wholesalers seeking to modernize operations, streamline quote-to-order workflows, and build stronger customer relationships. Here’s why wholesale businesses choose HubSpot:
Ready to transform wholesale operations? Start with HubSpot’s free tools with CRM functionality, then add advanced sales, marketing, service, automation, and commerce features as the business grows.
Editor's note: This post was originally published in July 2025 and has been updated for comprehensiveness.

title: Where Search Attention Is Going & How To Measure It via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
content:
Katie Morton, editor-in-chief of Search Engine Journal, and I recorded the debut episode of Search Engine Journal’s revamped podcast, focusing on a recurring theme in our coverage. We discussed how clicks are declining on the open web , a trend many in search have noticed. We argue that much of this attention hasn’t vanished but has shifted to areas not easily tracked by standard analytics. Listen to the complete episode here.
[04 : 28] — Introduction: The Disappearing Clicks [05 : 09] — Where to Invest Your Marketing Resources? [09 : 14] — How to Measure Performance Beyond Clicks [13 : 49] — Where Is Search Traffic Going? [16 : 41] — What Does Visibility Mean Now? [21 : 11] — Resetting Goals for Content Leaders
Most searches nowadays often don’t lead directly to a click on the open web. According to Rand Fishkin’s analysis of Similarweb clickstream data, about 68% of U.S. Google searches in the first four months of 2026 end without any click at all. Only around a quarter actually take users to an external website. The rest either conclude without a click, lead to another Google search, or direct users to a Google-owned property or paid result.
That attention is collecting in a few places. A lot of it never leaves Google, held by AI Overviews , Business Profiles, Maps listings, and newer surfaces like Ask Maps that point people toward specific businesses. Community platforms are showing up in the results more often, too.
After May’s core update , SE Ranking’s tracking showed Reddit gaining top-three positions across all 20 niches it follows. Google’s partnership with Reddit has been in place for a while, and Google has leaned harder into forum results, though I wouldn’t say the deal alone explains the movement.
Then there’s a narrower set of sites that still reliably pull organic traffic. Transactional, local, and branded searches keep sending clicks. What’s getting hit hardest is lifestyle content, wire-service journalism, and utility pages like weather and TV listings, which are the kind of thing an AI Overview can answer without sending a click anywhere.
Katie added that much of what leaves the open web lands on social platforms and video, where AI can’t easily replicate the formats. Younger audiences, in particular, are spending their time there rather than on traditional sites, and YouTube holds their attention across age ranges.
Many blogs try to cover every related topic with generic content, which worked when Google indexed them all and drove traffic. Now, they face tougher competition from similar pages and AI summaries that answer directly in search results. Focusing on volume alone no longer works.
Google’s Danny Sullivan drew that line at Search Central Live Toronto this spring , separating commodity content from the kind of work only your business and your experience can produce. The listicle that could come from anywhere sits on one side. What only you can say sits on the other. The topic matters less than which side of that line your content falls on.
John Mueller made a related point on Reddit . For a new site, the audience work comes first, and search visibility may follow once you’ve built something worth finding. Starting with “how do I rank” is the wrong place to start.
Katie tied this back to business fit. SEJ doesn’t take every client who waves money, because off-topic or low-quality sponsors can cost you your audience’s trust. For her, it stayed simple:
It always comes down to authenticity. You want to provide value, you want to serve your audience. It has to be this mutually beneficial thing.
Old-school SEO principles never die, and firsthand experience is the one thing AI can’t replicate.
The challenge now is that the numbers you once relied on have become harder to interpret. Raw traffic used to be a clear indicator, but today, your brand can appear throughout search results and still not show up in your analytics, especially if it didn’t lead to a click.
Branded search is a signal to monitor alongside citation tracking. Repeated exposure in AI answers may lead to more branded queries. Search Console’s branded queries filter makes these changes easier to identify.
Another change involves shifting from links to mentions. Unlinked mentions may matter in ways that a typical link report can’t detect. For example, a brand might be referenced in a Reddit thread, which a chatbot later relies on for a recommendation, even though there’s no hyperlink in the chain. If you only count links, you might overlook this.
Katie described the reader’s side from shopping for merino wool travel clothes:
I’m seeing brand names, but I’m not always clicking during the research process. I’m seeing brand names mentioned over again on the SERP and Reddit and in Claude, my preferred AI chatbot … eventually it will trigger a branded search, and then I’ll go directly to someone’s website, and they would probably have no idea how I found them.
That’s the attribution gap a lot of ecommerce is living in: Direct traffic they can’t tie back to a source. Her advice was to track where you’re being cited, keep a brand presence on Reddit, and make your content crawlable by AI.
No click doesn’t mean no value. Our argument on the episode was that if your content helped form the answer someone got, you may be in the consideration set even when no referral follows.
Katie emphasized that proving value as a content leader begins with identifying your “north star.” She pointed out that revenue and the bottom line are central, but it’s equally important for editorial and marketing to work hand in hand with the business strategy while still putting the audience first. Ultimately, it involves keeping content aligned with the business model, which also means being selective about customers to maintain the audience’s respect.
Part of the strategy involves niching down. SEJ improved its contributor program by becoming more selective about writers, prioritizing genuine expertise over self-promotion.
My piece of this is the scoreboard. When clicks stop being the main number, you make the clicks you do get count for more. If the only metric you report is organic sessions, and Google’s sending a smaller share of searches to the open web, that line is going to keep sliding. Keep the declining sessions in view and set them alongside the growing signals, like branded search queries and mentions.
This leaves content teams with a harder measurement job, and a more honest one.
A wider scoreboard can highlight value that a sessions-only report might miss. While it won’t undo the revenue loss caused by traffic that doesn’t return, managing both aspects together is truly the key to success now.
